Helper T cells only act after they see peptide presented on MHC class II, and CD4-positive, alpha-beta T cell activation is the transition from a resting naive cell to a proliferating, cytokine-secreting effector. It underwrites nearly all adaptive immunity, licensing B cell antibody responses and macrophage killing, while its miscalibration produces autoimmunity, allergy, or, when blunted, susceptibility to intracellular pathogens. Antigen recognition through class II molecules such as HLA-DRA and HLA-DRB1 is reinforced by costimulation from CD80, CD86, ICOS and OX40 ligand, and restrained by checkpoint ligands including PD-L1 and VISTA; signals converge on PKC-theta, MALT1 and NF-kB, mTOR, and JAK1/JAK3-STAT modules driven by IL-2, IL-6, IL-12, IL-21 and IL-23. Lineage-defining transcription factors -- TBX21, GATA3, RORC, BCL6, FOXP3 and ZBTB7B -- then fix the helper subset, with SOCS proteins, the RC3H ubiquitin ligases and proteasome subunits limiting the response.

The intestinal epithelium is renewed every few days from stem cells in the crypt base, and intestinal stem cell homeostasis is the balance that keeps their numbers steady — enough proliferation to replace shed enterocytes, not so much that crypts hyperplase or transform. Loss of that balance underlies impaired mucosal repair, chronic inflammation and colorectal tumour initiation. The genes here touch several inputs to that balance: LGR4 potentiates Wnt signalling from Paneth and mesenchymal niche cells, the dominant driver of crypt stem cell self-renewal; NOD2 senses bacterial muramyl dipeptide and links microbial cues to stem cell survival, with variants predisposing to Crohn's disease; membrane lipid handling through LPCAT3 and secreted phospholipases shapes crypt lipid composition and antimicrobial defence; and ZNHIT1 acts in chromatin remodelling that constrains the stem cell state. Together they place niche signalling, microbial sensing and lipid metabolism upstream of epithelial renewal.

Sustained neurotransmission depends on the local reuse of synaptic vesicle membrane, and one route to regeneration passes through an endosomal intermediate rather than returning directly to the releasable pool. After clathrin-mediated retrieval at the periactive zone, vesicle membrane fuses with a sorting endosome, where cargo composition is corrected before budding, re-acidification and refilling with neurotransmitter. Adaptor and small GTPase machinery gives the route its identity: an AP-3 subunit selects cargo for budding from endosomes, Rab7 marks the late endosomal compartment, intersectins couple endocytic sites to actin and GTPase regulators, and a GRIP-associated guanine nucleotide exchange factor links receptor and vesicle traffic to endosomal recycling. This slower pathway maintains vesicle protein quality and pool size during prolonged activity; its disruption is associated with impaired transmitter loading, presynaptic depression and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Locomotion covers the self-propelled movement of cells and whole organisms from one place to another, and in humans it is mostly cell migration: leukocytes crossing vessel walls to reach infection, endothelial tips sprouting new vessels, neural crest and axonal growth cones navigating the embryo, keratinocytes closing a wound, and sperm swimming. Its failure leaves immunodeficiency, defective vascular and neural patterning and poor healing, while its inappropriate reactivation underlies tumour invasion and metastasis. The genes span the layers this requires: chemokines and their receptors, growth factor and semaphorin/slit/ephrin guidance cues, integrins, cadherins and matrix components that provide traction, metalloproteinases that clear a path, and Rho-family GTPases with their regulators, actin nucleators, cofilin, profilin and myosin light-chain kinase that build and retract the leading edge. Ciliary and flagellar components add motile cilia and sperm propulsion, and numerous microRNAs and transcription factors tune the whole programme.

Cocaine blocks monoamine reuptake, and the cellular and behavioural changes that follow constitute the response to cocaine: acute reward, sensitisation with repeated exposure, and the lasting adaptations that underlie addiction and relapse. The immediate targets are present here as the dopamine and serotonin transporters, together with the full set of dopamine receptors, a serotonin receptor and degradative enzymes such as catechol-O-methyltransferase, which set how long released monoamines act. Downstream, striatal medium spiny neurons convert receptor signalling into changed gene expression through DARPP-32, CDK5, CREB and the long-lived transcription factor FosB, with DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase activity giving the response its persistence. Glutamatergic remodelling via AMPA receptors, Homer scaffolds and astrocytic glutamate transporters, plus stress and neuropeptide signalling through corticotropin-releasing hormone, oxytocin, nociceptin and the kappa-opioid receptor, links drug exposure to craving and negative affect in withdrawal.

During gastrulation, epiblast cells must decide whether to become mesoderm, and this regulatory layer sets how many do so, where, and when. The outcome determines the heart, blood, skeleton and muscle that later derive from mesoderm, and misregulation produces axis duplication, failed primitive streak formation or absent cardiac progenitors. Control is exerted largely by extracellular signals and their tuning: WNT3A drives streak formation while the secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2 restrain WNT signalling to limit the mesodermal domain, BMP receptor signalling through BMPR1A patterns posterior and extraembryonic mesoderm, and FGFR1 is required for cells to ingress through the streak and adopt mesodermal identity. Downstream, the transcription factor MESP1 marks and specifies nascent cardiovascular mesoderm. The same signalling logic is exploited to steer pluripotent stem cells toward mesodermal lineages in culture.

Penile erection is the vascular and smooth-muscle response that permits copulation: arterial inflow into the corpus cavernosum rises while venous outflow is restricted, so the erectile tissue engorges, stiffens and becomes erect. It is a neurovascular reflex integrating central arousal signals with local control of cavernosal smooth muscle tone, and its failure produces erectile dysfunction, a common consequence of diabetic and atherosclerotic vascular disease and of autonomic nerve injury. The genes here point to that mixture of inputs: oxytocin acts as a central and spinal pro-erectile neuropeptide, endothelin receptor signalling and purinergic P2Y1 receptor activation on endothelium and smooth muscle set vasoconstrictor and vasodilator balance, and adenosine deaminase shapes the pool of adenosine acting as a local relaxant. The process links autonomic signalling, endothelial function and reproductive physiology.

Helper T cell fate is as much a matter of restraint as of instruction, and this pathway covers the brakes applied to CD4-positive alpha-beta T cell differentiation. Limiting how readily naive CD4 cells commit, and blocking entry into the wrong effector programme, keeps the balance between Th1, Th2, Th17 and regulatory outputs appropriate to an infection and prevents autoimmune or allergic pathology. The machinery is largely transcriptional and post-transcriptional: RUNX1 and RUNX3 with their CBFB partner, BCL6, the CD4/CD8 lineage factor ZBTB7B, and FOXP3, which enforces a regulatory rather than conventional effector identity; TBX21 commits toward Th1 while excluding alternatives. Cytokine signalling is dampened by SOCS5 and by SMAD7 acting on TGF-beta responses, while the RNA-binding proteins RC3H1, RC3H2 and ZC3H12A degrade transcripts encoding costimulatory and cytokine drivers, and galectin-1 and annexin A1 impose extrinsic limits.

Pigmentation covers how melanin and related pigments accumulate in skin, hair, eyes and inner ear, whether by making more pigment per cell or by generating more pigment cells. It determines visible colour, shields keratinocyte DNA from ultraviolet damage, and supports retinal and cochlear function; its failure gives albinism, Waardenburg and Hermansky-Pudlak syndromes, piebaldism and hearing loss, while dysregulated melanocyte growth underlies melanoma. Melanoblasts arise from neural crest under MITF, SOX10 and KIT signalling, then build melanosomes as lysosome-related organelles: tyrosinase and TYRP1 catalyse melanin synthesis, PMEL forms the internal matrix, and OCA2 and SLC45A2 set organelle pH and ion balance. Adaptor and biogenesis complexes together with Rab GTPases deliver cargo to maturing melanosomes, and myosin Va with RAB27A and melanophilin captures them for transfer to neighbouring cells. Melanocortin receptor signalling opposed by agouti protein tunes the pigment type produced.

Hearing depends on a fixed, non-renewable set of cochlear hair cells, and this pathway controls how many of them are made and where. It governs the decision, taken in the developing organ of Corti, between becoming a mechanosensory hair cell and becoming a supporting cell. The proneural transcription factor ATOH1 drives hair cell fate and is both necessary and sufficient for it; lateral inhibition through a Notch receptor and its DLL1 ligand restricts that fate to a spaced subset, with HES1, HES5 and HEY2 acting as repressors that damp ATOH1 in neighbouring cells. MYCN and MYCL sustain progenitor proliferation before differentiation, and ESRP1 shapes epithelial splicing programmes in the same tissue. Loss or imbalance of these regulators produces extra, missing or disordered hair cells and congenital sensorineural deafness, and reactivating the module is a central strategy in hair cell regeneration research.

Lipogenesis is switched up when cells have surplus carbon or need membrane and storage lipids, and this is the set of influences that push fatty acid biosynthesis harder rather than performing the condensation chemistry itself. Its output matters for hepatic triglyceride accumulation, adipose expansion, milk and sebum lipid supply, and surfactant production; excessive drive contributes to fatty liver and dyslipidaemia. Transcriptional activators dominate: the carbohydrate-responsive factor MLXIPL couples glucose availability to lipogenic gene expression, while the liver X receptors NR1H2 and NR1H3 sense sterols and induce fatty acid synthesis alongside cholesterol efflux; MID1IP1 acts to stabilise acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity. Elongation and remodelling enzymes such as ELOVL5 and LPGAT1 extend the products. Also present are lipoprotein-associated apolipoproteins including APOA5 and APOC2, inflammatory mediators such as IL1B and PTGS2, and acetylation-dependent regulators, linking nutrient state and inflammation to lipid synthetic flux.

Paraxial mesoderm is the band of tissue flanking the neural tube that gives rise to somites and, from them, to the vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis of the trunk. Its morphogenesis is the shaping and organization of that tissue: presomitic mesoderm must be specified, held in an epithelializing state, and segmented in register with the body axis. Wnt ligands including WNT3A, WNT5A and WNT11 supply the posterior growth and patterning cues, with LEF1 transducing canonical Wnt input to transcription, while the paralogous forkhead factors FOXC1 and FOXC2 act together to set somite boundaries and sclerotome identity. Receptor serine/threonine kinase signalling of the TGF-beta superfamily and SMAD2/SMAD3-dependent transcription contribute further positional information, and vesicle-trafficking and actin-regulatory components support the cell rearrangements involved. Disruption produces axial skeletal malformations, fused or absent vertebrae, and defective muscle and skeletal patterning.

Sour taste detection lets an animal recognize acids, warning it away from spoiled or unripe food while contributing to the appreciation of fermented and citrus flavours. The genes here encode acid- and ion-sensitive channels of the taste bud: a candidate sour receptor formed by the polycystin-family subunits PKD2L1 and PKD1L3, which marks a distinct population of type III taste cells, together with acid-sensing ion channels of the ASIC family and the subunits of the epithelial sodium channel, ENaC, which is better established as the amiloride-sensitive salt-taste sensor. Protons entering or acting on these channels depolarize the receptor cell, triggering transmitter release onto gustatory afferents that carry the signal to the brainstem and cortex. This sensory transduction step is the entry point for reflexive rejection of acidic foods and for behavioural regulation of acid and electrolyte intake.

Smooth muscle cells are not terminally fixed: they switch between a contractile state and a proliferative, synthetic state, and this control arm holds differentiation back so that vessels and visceral muscle can grow, remodel and repair. Loss of the brake contributes to vascular disease, since the balance between contractile marker expression and dedifferentiation governs neointima formation after injury and the fate of cells in atherosclerotic plaques. Growth factors such as PDGFB and FGF9 and Notch effectors HEY1 and HEY2 suppress the contractile programme, calcineurin-NFAT signalling with its regulator RCAN1 feeds into the same decision, and epigenetic repressors including DNMT1, MECP2 and the methyltransferase PRDM6 silence differentiation genes. Several microRNAs act here as post-transcriptional switches, tuning how strongly progenitors and existing smooth muscle commit to the contractile phenotype during development and vascular remodelling.

Chromosomes segregate accurately only if each kinetochore is captured by microtubules from the correct spindle pole, and this pathway governs how strongly and how selectively those attachments form. Its output feeds the spindle assembly checkpoint: erroneous or tensionless connections are detached and the cell held in mitosis until they are corrected, so loss of control produces lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability typical of tumours. The chromosomal passenger complex — Aurora B kinase with INCENP, survivin and borealin — phosphorylates outer kinetochore substrates to destabilise improper attachments, while CDK1–cyclin B sets mitotic timing and NEK2 acts at centrosomes and kinetochores. Checkpoint and attachment components such as ZW10, ZWILCH, KNTC1 and the astrin partner KNSTRN report or stabilise the microtubule interface, and acetyltransferase and sirtuin activities tune the process.

Most of the skeleton is made twice: a cartilage model is laid down first and then replaced by bone, and endochondral bone morphogenesis is that conversion. It sets limb and vertebral length, drives postnatal growth at the physis, and its disruption produces chondrodysplasias, short stature and defective fracture healing. Chondrocytes commit under SOX9 and secrete a matrix of collagen II, matrilin and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein; proliferation and the pace of hypertrophy are timed by Indian hedgehog, CNP signalling through its guanylyl cyclase receptor NPR2, and FGF18 acting on FGFR3. Hypertrophic cells then mineralize with the help of alkaline phosphatase, invite vascular and osteoclast invasion, and matrix metalloproteinases clear the cartilage scaffold while RUNX2-dependent osteoblasts deposit collagen I bone. BMP and TGF-beta receptors, retinoic acid receptors and ciliary transport components tune each transition.

Salivary glands form by branching morphogenesis, in which an epithelial bud invades surrounding mesenchyme and repeatedly divides and clefts to build the ductal tree and secretory end buds. The epithelial cell proliferation that drives submandibular gland morphogenesis is what supplies the cells for that expansion, and its timing determines how large and how branched the final gland becomes; too little leaves a hypoplastic gland with impaired saliva production, dry mouth and poor oral and dental health. Mesenchymal FGF10 acting on epithelial FGFR2 is the central proliferative signal, with hedgehog signalling through SHH and the homeodomain factor NKX3-1 contributing to epithelial growth and duct patterning, and TNF-family signalling modulating the response. This is a classic instance of reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal induction, the same logic used in lung, kidney and mammary branching.

The heart must build its own blood supply, and coronary vasculature morphogenesis is the developmental programme that generates and patterns those vessels, converting scattered endothelial precursors into a hierarchical arterial, capillary and venous network that perfuses the growing myocardium. Without it the compact myocardium cannot be sustained, and defective coronary patterning underlies congenital anomalies such as coronary artery fistulae and contributes to outflow tract and aortic arch malformations. Growth factor signalling drives the process: VEGFA with its co-receptor NRP1 and FGF2 promote endothelial sprouting, PDGFRB recruits mural cells to stabilize nascent vessels, and TGF-beta receptor signalling shapes vessel wall assembly. NOTCH1 with the target HEY2 specifies arterial identity, while transcription factors including HAND2, TBX1 and TBX5 supply the cardiac positional information that tells vessels where to form.

Sister chromatids must stay glued together at their centromeres from replication until anaphase, and centromeric sister chromatid cohesion is the process that keeps them so. It matters because premature loss of centromeric cohesion produces unequal chromosome segregation, aneuploid daughter cells and, in oocytes, the chromosome missegregation behind trisomy and age-related infertility. The shugoshin proteins SGO1 and SGO2 mark the inner centromere and recruit a PP2A phosphatase holoenzyme, whose scaffolding subunits PPP2R1A and PPP2R1B appear here, to keep the cohesin ring dephosphorylated and protected from cleavage. The kinase BUB1 phosphorylates centromeric histone H2A to place shugoshin there, linking cohesion protection to the spindle assembly checkpoint and kinetochore geometry; MEIKIN adapts the system for the stepwise, two-division cohesion loss of meiosis. N-terminal acetylation by NAA10/NAA50 and the accessory factor BOD1 tune the same centromeric machinery.

Follicle-stimulating hormone acts on gonadal somatic cells to drive ovarian follicle growth and Sertoli cell support of spermatogenesis, and this pathway covers what a target cell does once the hormone arrives. Binding to the FSH receptor, a G protein-coupled receptor coupled to cAMP production, changes gene expression, steroidogenic capacity and paracrine output; loss of receptor signalling causes hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, follicle arrest and infertility, while its regulation sets the ovarian response in assisted reproduction. Downstream effectors here include the inhibin/activin subunit INHBA, which feeds back on pituitary FSH secretion, endothelin-1 with its receptor EDNRA acting on follicular and vascular tone, Notch and ephrin components mediating cell-cell contacts within the follicle, cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase supporting steroid hydroxylation, and the glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits that build glutathione against oxidative stress during follicular maturation.

Secreted growth factors would diffuse away from their site of production without something to hold them in place, and this pathway describes how proteins are anchored and kept within the extracellular region rather than allowed to disperse. The genes involved are largely devoted to sequestering TGF-beta superfamily ligands: fibrillins build the microfibrils of elastic fibres and connective tissue, latent TGF-beta binding protein tethers the latent growth factor complex to that matrix scaffold, and NRROS retains latent TGF-beta1 at the cell surface, notably in microglia. Cerberus and its relative DAND5, together with NBL1, bind BMP and Nodal-family ligands extracellularly and restrict where they can act, shaping embryonic axis and left-right patterning. Loss of fibrillin disrupts this reservoir function and causes connective tissue disease with excess TGF-beta signalling, illustrating that spatial confinement of a ligand is itself a form of regulation.

Programmed cell death of macrophages sets the size and lifespan of tissue phagocyte populations and determines whether an inflammatory lesion resolves or persists. Because macrophages are long-lived sentinels that ingest pathogens and debris, their survival must be tuned to the signals they encounter: infection, cholesterol loading, and cytokine withdrawal all push them toward apoptosis, and in atherosclerotic plaques macrophage death drives necrotic core formation. The genes here connect innate immune sensing to that decision, including a bacterial peptidoglycan sensor, interferon-regulatory transcription factors downstream of nucleic acid sensing, and a chemokine-receptor pair that supports survival. Others act as brakes or accelerators: a NAD-dependent deacetylase and a cell cycle inhibitor of the CDKN2A locus, a lysosomal protease whose release permeabilizes membranes, an ER-resident selenoprotein guarding against ER stress, and a microRNA restraining inflammatory output.

Formation of the distal convoluted tubule gives the nephron the segment that fine-tunes salt balance after the loop of Henle, reabsorbing a small but tightly regulated fraction of filtered sodium through the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter and handling calcium and magnesium transport. Because this segment sets the final composition of urine, defects in its specification or function underlie salt-wasting and blood pressure disorders. Patterning depends on nuclear factors that establish and maintain renal epithelial identity: paired-box regulators drive nephron progenitor commitment and tubule epithelialisation, and a POU-domain factor directs regional identity along the proximal-distal axis of the developing nephron. Maturation is marked by segment-restricted products such as the calcium-binding protein calbindin and, in the adjoining thick ascending limb, uromodulin. The programme is one part of nephrogenesis, linking kidney morphogenesis to lifelong electrolyte homeostasis.

Bone resorption is carried out by large multinucleated cells, and this fusion step is how they are made: mononuclear osteoclast precursors of the monocyte/macrophage lineage merge their plasma membranes to form a single syncytium capable of sealing onto bone and dissolving mineral and matrix. Multinucleation gives the cell the size and cytoskeletal organisation needed for an effective resorptive apparatus, so blocking it reduces bone loss, while excessive fusion accompanies the osteolysis of osteoporosis, inflammatory arthritis and bone metastasis. Fusion is driven downstream of RANKL and inflammatory signalling by dedicated surface molecules, including a transmembrane protein required specifically for precursor fusion and a tetraspanin that organises membrane microdomains, together with a podosome-associated adaptor linking membrane contact to actin remodelling. Transcriptional modulators tune how readily precursors commit to fusing.

The pace of the heartbeat is set by how quickly electrical impulses are generated in pacemaker tissue and propagated through the myocardium, and this pathway covers the ion channels and junctional proteins that tune that rate. Hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels, notably HCN4, carry the pacemaker current in sinoatrial cells; L- and T-type calcium channels support depolarization; and repolarization is shaped by potassium channels such as KCNQ1, KCNH2 and KCNJ2 together with their KCNE accessory subunits, while inward-rectifier channels coupled to muscarinic signalling slow the rate under vagal input. Sodium channel SCN5A with its beta subunits, the anchoring proteins ANK2 and AKAP9, and desmosomal and gap-junction components including PKP2, DSP and GJA5 position and connect these channels between cells. Mutations here produce long QT and Brugada syndromes, sick sinus syndrome, atrial fibrillation and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

Before a cell divides, every chromosome must be pulled to the spindle midzone and held there in a single plane; regulation of metaphase plate congression covers the inputs that tune how fast and how completely that alignment is achieved. Getting it right is what makes chromosome segregation accurate, and slippage produces lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability typical of tumours. Much of the control resides in the chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B kinase together with INCENP, survivin and borealin corrects improperly attached kinetochores, while CDK1 sets mitotic timing and MAD1L1 links alignment status to the spindle assembly checkpoint. Dynein-based transport, the spindle pole organiser NuMA and the microtubule-binding protein astrin contribute the mechanical and positional side, and acetyltransferase and sirtuin activities modulate the process, connecting congression to chromatin and tubulin modification.

NMDA-type glutamate receptors only support learning-related plasticity if they are concentrated at the postsynaptic membrane opposite a transmitter release site, and this clustering process is what puts them and holds them there. It links a trans-synaptic adhesion pair, neurexin on the presynaptic side and neuroligin on the postsynaptic side, to the scaffolding of the postsynaptic density, where SHANK3 anchors receptors within a dense protein lattice. Secreted cues contribute as well: reelin signalling through lipoprotein receptors, with apolipoprotein E as a competing ligand, tunes receptor subunit composition and positioning during circuit maturation. The result is a synapse capable of coincidence detection, calcium influx and long-term potentiation. Disruption of these adhesion and scaffold components is recurrent in autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia, and the reelin and APOE arms tie the same machinery to cortical development and to synaptic loss in neurodegeneration.

Every heartbeat begins with a cardiomyocyte action potential, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets its shape, duration and rate of firing rather than the depolarization itself. Its outputs are pacemaker automaticity and orderly conduction: HCN channels carry the funny current that drives sinoatrial diastolic depolarization, GJA5 forms the connexin channels through which excitation spreads, and L-type calcium entry through CACNA1C, coupled to RYR2 release and SERCA2 reuptake, links electrical activity to contraction. Calmodulin, CaMKII and NOS1AP tune channel behaviour, while anchoring and cytoskeletal proteins such as AKAP9, ANK2, BIN1 and CAV3 place channels at the membrane domains where they act. Desmosomal components including PKP2, DSP, DSG2 and JUP tie mechanical junctions to conduction. Mutations here underlie long QT and Brugada syndromes, sick sinus syndrome, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with sudden cardiac death.

Removal of the 5' cap commits an mRNA to destruction, and this decapping step sets how long a transcript survives and therefore how much protein it makes. It is the decisive event in the major cytoplasmic decay route: after deadenylation, the LSM1-7 ring and its partner PATL1 mark the shortened 3' end, and the DCP2 catalytic subunit, held in an active configuration by DCP1 and the scaffold EDC4 with EDC3 and DDX6, cleaves the cap to expose the body of the message to 5'-to-3' degradation by XRN1. Related Nudix-family hydrolases and DCPS handle cap dinucleotides and non-canonical caps, while ZFP36 and CAPRIN1 link sequence-specific RNA binding to this machinery. The reactions concentrate in processing bodies and underlie rapid shutoff of cytokine and cell cycle transcripts, quality control of aberrant RNAs, and translational silencing in oocytes and neurons.

Cytosolic double-stranded DNA, whether from bacteria, viruses or damaged host nuclei, nucleates the AIM2 inflammasome, and this control layer sets how readily that complex forms. Because assembly commits a cell to caspase-1 activation, IL-1β and IL-18 maturation and pyroptotic death, tuning it decides whether an infected cell is sacrificed or spared, and mistuning contributes to autoinflammatory tissue damage. Interferon-inducible guanylate-binding proteins act upstream by helping lyse pathogen-containing vacuoles and bacteria so that DNA reaches the cytosol, raising the amount of ligand available. IFI16 is a related DNA sensor of the same family that can also engage nuclear and cytoplasmic DNA, while pyrin-domain-only proteins act as decoys that block productive PYD-PYD polymerisation, and TRIM11 contributes ubiquitin-dependent regulation. The net effect is threshold-setting for innate immune detection of misplaced DNA.

Microglia and astrocytes must be able to switch off an inflammatory response once a threat has passed, and dampening the neuroinflammatory response is what keeps immune activity in the brain from damaging the tissue it protects. Neurons signal their health directly to microglia through ligand-receptor pairs such as CD200-CD200R1 and fractalkine, holding resident phagocytes in a quiescent state; loss of this restraint gives synapse loss, chronic gliosis and progressive neurodegeneration. Other components act inside the microglial cell, where progranulin, TREM2 and cystatin F set the threshold and duration of activation, and mutations in progranulin or TREM2 cause frontotemporal dementia and raise Alzheimer risk. Anti-inflammatory cytokine and growth factor input, a circadian transcriptional repressor, and several microRNAs add further layers of suppression, linking immune tone in the CNS to lipid handling, sleep-wake timing and repair.

Not every amino acid a cell makes is destined for protein; this route covers synthesis of amino acids that act as neurotransmitters, metabolic intermediates or structural modifications. Glutamate decarboxylases GAD1 and GAD2 generate GABA, the principal inhibitory transmitter, and serine racemase produces D-serine, the co-agonist at NMDA receptors, tying this chemistry directly to synaptic excitability; loss of GABA synthesis provokes seizures. Other members feed ornithine and citrulline production for the urea cycle and carbamoyl phosphate synthesis, while procollagen lysyl hydroxylases create hydroxylysine residues needed for collagen crosslinking, and their deficiency causes a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Transporters and catabolic enzymes such as ABAT and DPYD set the surrounding flux, so the pathway sits at the junction of nitrogen disposal, neurotransmission and extracellular matrix maturation.

Lactones are cyclic esters that arise from drugs, dietary plant compounds, bacterial signalling molecules and oxidative damage to lipids, and this pathway covers their handling — hydrolysis of the ring and the redox chemistry that accompanies it. The paraoxonase family provides the lactonase activity, with PON1 in plasma associated with HDL and linked to organophosphate detoxification and atherosclerosis risk, while PON2 acts intracellularly and can degrade bacterial quorum-sensing lactones. Glutathione supply and transfer enzymes, including the catalytic subunit of glutamate–cysteine ligase and omega-class glutathione transferases, support the thiol-dependent steps, and ascorbate handling appears through vitamin C transporters and the glucose carriers that import its oxidized lactone form, dehydroascorbate. Together these activities connect xenobiotic disposal to cellular antioxidant defence.

When DNA damage is severe enough that repair cannot rescue the cell, p53 directs the mitochondrial arm of apoptosis, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower the threshold for that decision. The balance matters because too little killing permits damaged cells to persist and become tumours, while too much sacrifices tissue after tolerable injury. Control is exerted at several levels: cofactors and chromatin regulators such as ING2, KDM1A and SIRT1 tune p53 activity through acetylation and methylation, TAF9 and TAF9B couple it to the transcription machinery, and RPL26 and HNRNPK act on p53 mRNA and protein output. Downstream, BCL2 and TRIAP1 restrain mitochondrial permeabilisation and caspase activation, while ZNF385A shapes which p53 target programme is selected. Signals from MIF, CD74, CD44 and MUC1 push the same axis toward survival, a route frequently exploited in cancer.

Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in the brain, and this pathway covers the processes that set how much of it is released at a synapse and how strongly the postsynaptic cell is driven. Tuning release matters because too little weakens cortical signalling and learning, while too much is excitotoxic; both extremes are implicated in schizophrenia and epilepsy. The genes here act at several levels: STXBP1 is required for the priming of synaptic vesicles for calcium-triggered fusion and its loss causes severe early infantile epileptic encephalopathy; RAB3GAP1 is the catalytic subunit of the Rab3 GTPase-activating complex, which stimulates GTP hydrolysis on Rab3 and so terminates its active state during the exocytotic cycle; DTNBP1 contributes to vesicle trafficking in glutamatergic terminals; SLC38A2 imports glutamine as precursor for transmitter resynthesis; and KMO diverts tryptophan metabolism toward kynurenines that modulate glutamate receptors.

When tissue is injured, the repair programme can either restore the original architecture or replace it with fibrous scar, and control over connective tissue replacement is what sets the balance. Excess replacement is fibrosis — stiffened lung, cirrhotic liver, remodelled heart after infarction — while too little leaves wounds mechanically weak. The protein members here act at distinct levels: ROCK1 and ROCK2 transduce Rho-dependent cytoskeletal tension into myofibroblast contractility and matrix production, the calcineurin catalytic subunit PPP3CA couples calcium signals to transcription, PPARG activation opposes fibroblast activation, RUNX1 drives lineage-specific transcriptional responses, and AGER senses advanced glycation end products and other damage-associated ligands. A large set of microRNAs, including the miR-15/16 and miR-34 families along with miR-17, miR-195, miR-199 and miR-214, dampens or reinforces these circuits post-transcriptionally, making scar formation a dose-controlled outcome rather than a switch.

When oxygen falls low enough that adaptation fails, cells can commit to death from within, and this hypoxia-triggered intrinsic apoptotic route is how that decision is transmitted to the mitochondrial execution machinery. It sets the threshold for cell loss in ischaemic tissue — infarcted myocardium, stroke penumbra, hypoxic tumour cores — and its suppression lets tumour cells survive an environment that should kill them. The balance is struck between pro-death and protective components: BNIP3 accumulates under hypoxia and permeabilises mitochondria, while ARC (NOL3) and the ER calcium-leak regulator TMBIM6 restrain caspase activation and limit calcium-driven death. PINK1 links the response to mitochondrial quality control, and kinase and lipid-kinase signalling through MAP2K1 and PIK3CB together with the transcription factor ATF2 determine whether hypoxic stress resolves in survival or apoptosis.

Cells hold potassium high inside and sodium high outside, and this uptake of potassium across the plasma membrane is what builds and maintains that gradient. On it depend the resting membrane potential, the excitability of neurons and muscle, cell volume regulation, and the reabsorption of salt and water in kidney and gut; loss of individual components causes cardiac arrhythmia, epilepsy, periodic paralysis, salt-wasting tubulopathies and hyperinsulinism. The Na+/K+-ATPase pump, built from catalytic alpha and glycosylated beta subunits and tuned by small FXYD regulators, drives uptake using ATP, while cation-chloride cotransporters bring potassium in with sodium and chloride under control of a WNK-responsive kinase. Inward-rectifying and other potassium channels, including ATP-sensitive channels paired with sulfonylurea receptors and hyperpolarization-activated pacemaker channels, allow inward flux that sets pacemaking and couples metabolism to secretion.

CXCL1 is a neutrophil-recruiting chemokine, and the signals that raise its output determine how quickly granulocytes arrive at an inflamed or infected tissue. Upregulation of CXCL1 production by epithelial cells, fibroblasts and synoviocytes drives protective antibacterial and antifungal responses at mucosal surfaces, but sustained induction contributes to the neutrophil-rich inflammation of psoriasis, arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease. The dominant input here is IL-17 family cytokine signalling: IL-17A and IL-17F acting through the IL-17RA receptor chain trigger NF-κB- and MAPK-dependent transcription of CXCL1 together with other neutrophil chemoattractants, and stabilise the resulting mRNA. Innate receptor signalling contributes through the TIRAP adaptor, which serves TLR2 and TLR4 responses to bacterial products. The mechanosensitive cation channel TRPV4 links mechanical and osmotic stress at the cell surface to the same chemokine output, tying tissue strain to leukocyte recruitment.

Cytotoxic CD8-positive alpha-beta T cells kill infected and transformed cells, and restraining their activation is what keeps that killing proportionate and self-tolerant. Damping this response prevents autoimmune tissue destruction and immunopathology during infection, but the same brakes are exploited by tumours to evade immune attack, which is why several members here are the targets of checkpoint blockade. The mechanisms are mixed: PD-L1 and VISTA are inhibitory ligands engaging receptors on the T cell surface; LILRB1 and HFE act through MHC class I recognition; SOCS1 shuts down cytokine receptor signalling from inside the cell; and ZBTB7B (ThPOK) suppresses the CD8 cytotoxic programme during thymic lineage choice, favouring CD4 helper commitment. Together these constitute co-inhibitory signalling, cytokine-signalling attenuation and developmental repression converging on cytotoxic T cell output.

Type I interferon alerts cells to viral infection, and the interferon alpha response is the transcriptional programme it switches on: dozens of genes that make a cell inhospitable to virus replication and better seen by the immune system. Signalling through STAT2 and IRF9 with IRF7 amplification drives effectors that act at every stage of the viral cycle — MX1 and IFITM proteins block entry and trafficking, OAS1 and EIF2AK2 shut down viral RNA and translation, BST2 tethers budding virions, and ISG15 with its conjugation machinery (UBA7, UBE2L6, HERC6) modifies host and viral proteins, while USP18 removes the mark and restrains the response. Immunoproteasome subunits and TAP1 with HLA class I raise antigen presentation, and CXCL10/CXCL11 recruit lymphocytes. Sustained or misdirected activation of this programme underlies interferonopathies and contributes to lupus-like autoimmunity.

Monoamine neurotransmitters and dietary amines are cleared by oxidative deamination to their corresponding aldehydes, the reaction carried out by the two flavin-dependent monoamine oxidases MAOA and MAOB on the outer mitochondrial membrane. This step terminates signalling by serotonin, dopamine, noradrenaline and related amines, protects tissues from vasoactive amines such as tyramine absorbed from food, and generates hydrogen peroxide as a by-product that contributes to oxidative stress in neurons. The two isoforms are closely related and share many substrates, but MAOA acts preferentially on serotonin while MAOB favours phenylethylamine, and their tissue distributions differ. Because inhibiting these enzymes raises synaptic amine levels, they are long-standing drug targets in depression and in Parkinson disease; loss of MAOA function in humans causes a syndrome of amine accumulation with impulsive aggression. The aldehyde products are further metabolised by aldehyde dehydrogenases and reductases.

An integrated HIV-1 provirus is transcribed by the host's own RNA polymerase II machinery, so viral gene expression is essentially a hijacking of cellular transcription, and the balance between silence and activity at the viral promoter determines whether an infected cell stays latent or produces virus. Sequences in the 5' long terminal repeat recruit TBP and the TAF-containing general factors, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and the TFIIH helicase-kinase module, which positions polymerase and phosphorylates its C-terminal domain. Polymerase then pauses just downstream, held by NELF and DSIF; escape into productive elongation requires the viral Tat protein binding the nascent TAR stem-loop and recruiting P-TEFb (CDK9 with cyclin T1). Capping enzymes, the nuclear cap-binding complex, elongin and ELL elongation factors, and the FACT histone chaperone complete the cycle, yielding transcripts that serve as mRNA and as packaged genomic RNA.

Growth factor signalling through ERK must be switched off as well as on, and this is the shut-off arm: phosphatases strip the activating phosphates from the Thr-Xaa-Tyr motif in the activation loop of ERK1, ERK2 and ERK5, returning the kinases to a resting state. Because ERK activity drives proliferation, differentiation and survival gene programmes, the duration and amplitude of the signal determine the cellular outcome, and loss of this braking step contributes to unchecked mitogenic signalling in cancer. Dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP6 and DUSP7, which act largely on ERK in the cytoplasm, and nuclear DUSP4, remove both phosphates, while the PP2A holoenzyme built from catalytic, scaffolding and B56 regulatory subunits contributes serine/threonine dephosphorylation; VRK3 acts as a scaffold promoting phosphatase action on ERK. Since ERK itself induces DUSP transcription, the arrangement forms a negative feedback loop.

Neurotrophin binding to the p75 neurotrophin receptor turns the receptor's cytoplasmic tail into a docking platform, and the complexes it recruits determine whether a neuron survives, grows, or dies. Because p75NTR has no catalytic activity of its own, everything depends on which adaptors arrive: here the assembly built around NGF-bound receptor gathers RIPK2, MYD88 and IRAK1 together with the scaffold p62 and atypical protein kinase C iota, converging on TRAF6. TRAF6 acts as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, and the polyubiquitin supplied by the ubiquitin genes in this module drives activation of the IKK complex through IKBKB, freeing NF-kB to enter the nucleus and switch on survival and inflammatory transcription. This arm of neurotrophin signalling opposes the pro-apoptotic outputs of the same receptor, and its balance shapes developmental neuronal pruning, axon growth and injury responses.

Pancreatic endocrine cells arise from a transient population of progenitors that switch on neurogenin 3, and this transcriptional programme is what commits those cells away from duct and acinar fates toward the hormone-producing islet lineages. Without it no beta, alpha, delta or PP cells form; loss-of-function mutations in humans cause congenital malabsorptive diarrhoea with permanent neonatal diabetes, and the same programme is the target of efforts to make beta cells from stem cells. NEUROG3 acts as a short-lived pioneer factor that directly induces a second tier of regulators, including PAX4, NEUROD1, NKX2-2 and the zinc-finger factor INSM1, which together consolidate endocrine identity, drive exit from the cell cycle, and bias progenitors toward particular hormone subtypes. The pathway illustrates how a brief pulse of one factor is converted into a stable differentiated state.

Growth factor binding to the EGF receptor does more than switch on kinase cascades; one branch of its output runs through phospholipid turnover, and that is what this pathway captures. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or heparin-binding EGF — dimerises and autophosphorylates the receptor, creating docking sites that recruit phospholipase C-gamma1 through its SH2 domains. Once tyrosine phosphorylated at the membrane, PLCG1 cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, so a single receptor event raises cytosolic calcium released from internal stores and activates protein kinase C. The resulting calcium and PKC signals feed into proliferation, migration and cytoskeletal remodelling in epithelia, and inappropriate output from this arm contributes to the growth and invasiveness of EGFR-driven carcinomas.

Cancer-associated mutations at arginine 132 of the cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase IDH1 convert a routine metabolic step into the production of an oncometabolite. Wild-type IDH1 oxidatively decarboxylates isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while reducing NADP+, supplying both a citric acid cycle intermediate and cytosolic NADPH for redox defence and lipid synthesis. The mutant enzyme instead reduces 2-oxoglutarate using NADPH to give 2-hydroxyglutarate, which builds up to millimolar levels in the cytosol. Because 2-hydroxyglutarate closely resembles 2-oxoglutarate, it competitively inhibits dioxygenases that depend on it, including histone and DNA demethylases and prolyl hydroxylases, producing the hypermethylated, differentiation-blocked state characteristic of IDH1-mutant tumours. The alteration is frequent in gliomas and glioblastomas and also occurs in acute myeloid leukaemia, and it serves both as a diagnostic marker and as a drug target for mutant-selective inhibitors.

Every round of protein synthesis in the cytoplasm begins with charging a tRNA with its matching amino acid, and cytosolic tRNA aminoacylation is the step that establishes the accuracy of the genetic code. A family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, one for most amino acids plus a bifunctional glutamyl-prolyl enzyme, activates the amino acid with ATP and transfers it to the 3' end of a nuclear-encoded tRNA, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate; a pyrophosphatase removes the latter to keep the reaction favourable. Eight of these enzymes assemble with the accessory factors AIMP1, AIMP2 and EEF1E1 into a multi-synthetase complex thought to channel charged tRNAs to translating ribosomes, and several components moonlight in angiogenesis, inflammation and DNA damage signalling. Mutations in individual synthetases such as GARS1 and AARS1 cause peripheral neuropathies and multisystem developmental disorders, reflecting how narrowly translation tolerates mischarging.

Leukocytes find their way to infection, injury and lymphoid tissue by reading gradients of secreted chemoattractant proteins, and the binding of chemokines to their G protein-coupled receptors is the recognition step that sets that migration in motion. Ligands of the CC, CXC, CX3C and XC families engage matching receptors such as CCR1-CCR10, CXCR1-CXCR6, CX3CR1 and XCR1, triggering calcium flux, integrin activation and directed chemotaxis. The pairings define immune cell behaviour: CCR7 with CCL19 and CCL21 routes dendritic cells and naive T cells into lymph nodes, CXCR4 with CXCL12 retains progenitors in bone marrow, and CXCR1/CXCR2 with CXCL8 recruits neutrophils to inflamed tissue. Atypical receptors including ACKR2, ACKR3 and ACKR4 bind ligands without conventional signalling, scavenging them to shape gradients. This signalling underlies inflammation, lymphoid organisation, HIV entry and tumour metastasis.

Dolichol kinase converts dolichol to dolichyl phosphate in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, the lipid carrier on which the oligosaccharide precursor for N-linked glycosylation is built and which also supplies O-mannosylation and GPI anchor synthesis. When DOLK activity is lost, dolichyl phosphate becomes limiting and glycan transfer to nascent proteins fails across many substrates at once, producing the underglycosylated serum glycoproteins that define a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation. The resulting DOLK-CDG is a severe multisystem disease, with dilated cardiomyopathy, ichthyosis, seizures, hypotonia and developmental failure, and death frequently occurs in infancy. Because the affected step sits upstream of all dolichol-dependent glycosylation rather than within one glycan branch, the defect illustrates how a single lipid-activating kinase governs secretory protein maturation, membrane protein folding and cell surface anchoring throughout the body.

Death receptor engagement can end in either apoptosis or necroptosis, and caspase-8 is the switch that decides. When its proteolytic activity is blocked, the cell dies by regulated necrosis instead, because caspase-8 normally cleaves RIPK1 and RIPK3 and so dismantles the kinase complex that drives that route. The suppression of caspase-8 activity therefore matters for inflammation and antiviral defence: viruses encode FLIP-like proteins, and the endogenous short FLIP isoform encoded by CFLAR likewise occupies the caspase-8 dimerisation partner site, converting the death-inducing platform into a necroptotic one. Ligands such as FASLG and TRAIL acting through FAS and the TRAIL receptors recruit FADD, which brings procaspase-8 into a complex where it must dimerise and self-process to become a functional heterotetramer; pan-caspase inhibitors block that step with the same consequence.

CFTR is a cAMP-regulated chloride channel in the apical membrane of epithelia, and the chloride and bicarbonate it moves set the hydration and pH of airway, pancreatic, intestinal and biliary secretions. When mutation prevents the protein from folding, as with the common F508del allele, the channel never reaches the surface and cystic fibrosis follows: thick unclearable mucus and chronic lung infection, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus, biliary disease, salty sweat and male infertility. The genes here trace the fate of the misfolded protein rather than the channel's transport function — lectin-like ER quality control and retention factors such as OS9, ERLEC1 and the SEL1L complex, membrane ubiquitin ligases RNF5 and RNF185, the VCP ATPase and derlin channels that retrotranslocate the substrate, and the ubiquitin and 26S proteasome machinery that degrades it. Loss of function is thus a disposal problem imposed by endoplasmic-reticulum-associated degradation.

Pulmonary surfactant lowers surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface and keeps the lungs from collapsing at end-expiration, and ABCA3 is the lipid transporter that loads the phospholipids and cholesterol needed to build it into lamellar bodies of alveolar type II cells. There, lipids and surfactant proteins are packaged into bilayer stacks for secretion into the airspace. When ABCA3 function is lost, normal lamellar bodies fail to form and are replaced by small vesicles with electron-dense inclusions, surfactant secretion collapses, and lipoproteinaceous material accumulates in the alveoli. The resulting disorder of surfactant metabolism, pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 3, presents as severe and usually fatal neonatal respiratory distress, with milder mutations underlying childhood interstitial lung disease. This links ABC-transporter-mediated lipid translocation directly to lung development and neonatal respiratory physiology.

The mitotic cell cycle is the ordered programme by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, passing through G1, S, G2 and M with quiescence as an alternative exit. Its fidelity determines tissue growth and renewal, and its deregulation through cyclin, CDK inhibitor and retinoblastoma-pathway lesions is a hallmark of cancer. Cyclin-dependent kinases paired with D, E, A and B cyclins drive the transitions, restrained by CDK inhibitors, WEE1 and phosphatases and reset by ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis through SCF and the anaphase-promoting complex with the proteasome. Origin licensing on ORC and MCM proteins commits cells to replication; centrosome maturation, gamma-tubulin nucleation, kinetochore assembly, cohesin and condensin, spindle checkpoint surveillance, nuclear envelope and Golgi breakdown, and ESCRT-dependent abscission complete division.</description>}

Newly transcribed tRNAs are unusable until they are trimmed, tailed, spliced and chemically decorated, and tRNA processing is the set of reactions that converts precursors into functional adaptors for translation in both the nucleus and the mitochondrion. RNase P, whose catalytic RNA subunit works with protein partners, removes 5' leaders, ELAC2 cleaves 3' trailers, TRNT1 adds an untemplated CCA end, and the TSEN endonuclease complex with RTCB-containing ligase machinery excises and rejoins introns. A large family of modification enzymes then installs methyl, pseudouridine, thiol, queuosine and wybutosine groups, many at the anticodon loop where they set decoding accuracy and frameshift avoidance. Nucleoporins and exportin-t with RAN provide the nuclear export and retrograde traffic that couple processing to cytoplasmic use. In mitochondria the polycistronic transcript is cut to release rRNAs, mRNAs and tRNAs; defects cause mitochondrial disease, anaemia, microcephaly and neurodevelopmental syndromes.

Ribosomes are built from rRNA that must be carved out of long precursor transcripts, chemically modified, and folded together with ribosomal proteins before a subunit can translate anything. In the nucleolus, a single 47S precursor is trimmed by endonucleases and exonucleases into the 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs, with snoRNP-guided pseudouridylation and 2'-O-methylation plus base methylation and acetylation installed as cleavage proceeds. Large assemblies of processing factors, RNA helicases and the exosome complex act on the precursor, while the ribosomal proteins of the 40S and 60S subunits join and final maturation steps occur in the cytoplasm. A parallel set of enzymes processes and modifies the 12S and 16S rRNAs cut from mitochondrial polycistronic transcripts, supporting mitochondrial translation. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on cell growth, defects in these factors cause ribosomopathies such as bone marrow failure and craniofacial syndromes, and the pathway is heavily exploited by proliferating tumour cells.

Translation is the step where genetic information becomes protein, and this collection covers the whole of it: cytosolic initiation, elongation and termination, aminoacylation of tRNAs, co-translational targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum, and the separate translation system inside mitochondria. Cytosolic ribosomal subunits work with cap-binding and scaffolding initiation factors, the eIF2 complex and its guanine nucleotide exchange factor eIF2B, elongation factors eEF1A and eEF2, and release factor eRF1 with ABCE1 for recycling. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases exist as distinct cytosolic and mitochondrial enzymes, and mutations in either class cause neuropathies and mitochondrial disease. Signal recognition particle, its ER receptor, the Sec61 translocon and signal peptidase route secretory and membrane proteins into the ER. Mitoribosomal proteins, formylmethionine-tRNA machinery, TUFM and OXA1L build the thirteen hydrophobic respiratory chain subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Quality control components resolve stalled ribosomes and degrade aberrant nascent chains through ubiquitination and the proteasome.

Adenosine-to-inosine conversion is the most common form of RNA editing in humans, rewriting transcripts after they are made so that a single gene can yield proteins of different function. Because the ribosome reads inosine as guanosine, editing within coding sequence changes amino acids: the best-known case recodes a glutamine to arginine in the GluA2 AMPA receptor subunit, making the assembled receptor impermeable to calcium and protecting neurons from excitotoxic damage. Editing of serotonin 5-HT2C receptor transcripts similarly tunes G-protein coupling efficiency. The reaction is carried out by double-stranded RNA-specific adenosine deaminases, ADAR and ADARB1, which recognise duplex structure in pre-mRNA formed with complementary intronic sequence rather than a linear consensus. Activity is highest in brain, and beyond recoding, widespread editing of repetitive duplexes marks transcripts as self and restrains innate immune sensing of endogenous RNA.

Every collagen molecule begins as three polypeptide chains that must find each other and wind into a triple helix, and chain trimerization is the selection step that decides which chains pair with which. It determines whether a molecule becomes a fibril-forming type I or III collagen, a basement membrane type IV network, a beaded filament type VI, or an anchoring type VII, and errors here underlie osteogenesis imperfecta, chondrodysplasias, Alport syndrome and several epidermolysis bullosa forms. In fibrillar procollagens the C-propeptide drives the initial association, brings the chains into correct register and nucleates helix formation, which then propagates toward the N-terminus in zipper-like fashion; other family members use different C-terminal non-collagenous domains for the same purpose, and disulfide bonding stabilizes some trimers such as type III. Correct trimer composition sets the mechanical and adhesive properties of the extracellular matrix that follows.

Rather than build every nucleotide from scratch, cells recover the bases and nucleosides released by RNA and DNA turnover and phosphorylate them back into monophosphates that re-enter the nucleotide pools. This salvage route is far cheaper in energy than de novo synthesis and is the main supply for cells with limited biosynthetic capacity, such as neurons and lymphocytes, and for mitochondria, which must maintain their own deoxyribonucleotide pools. Phosphoribosyltransferases reattach purine bases to ribose phosphate, while kinases such as thymidine kinase, deoxycytidine kinase and deoxyguanosine kinase act on nucleosides; phosphorylases and deaminases run the catabolic side, degrading or interconverting bases. Loss of HPRT1 causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency, and mutations in the mitochondrial kinases produce mtDNA depletion syndromes. The same enzymes activate nucleoside analogue drugs.

Dietary fat absorbed by the small intestine cannot travel through blood or lymph unless it is packaged, and chylomicron assembly is the enterocyte process that builds those packages. Each nascent particle nucleates on a single molecule of apolipoprotein B-48, onto which microsomal triglyceride transfer protein — a heterodimer with protein disulfide isomerase — loads triacylglycerol, phospholipid and cholesterol as the apolipoprotein is translocated into the endoplasmic reticulum lumen. Exchangeable apolipoproteins A-I, A-II and A-IV join the surface, with apoC-II, apoC-III and apoE added or acquired to control later lipolysis by lipoprotein lipase and hepatic clearance of remnants. The particle then leaves the ER in specialized vesicles requiring the COPII component SAR1B before secretion into lymph. Loss of the transfer protein causes abetalipoproteinemia, and SAR1B defects cause chylomicron retention disease, both producing fat malabsorption and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.

Inflammation must be actively switched off, and the omega-3 fatty acid DPAn-3 is one substrate from which the lipid signals that do the switching are made. Its conversion into specialised proresolving mediators yields n-3 docosapentaenoic acid analogues of the resolvins, protectins and maresins built from DHA, which limit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and return tissue to homeostasis rather than merely blocking inflammatory signalling. DPAn-3 itself sits between EPA and DHA in the omega-3 elongation and desaturation route, so the same oxygenases act on it: lipoxygenases introduce oxygen at specific carbons to give hydroperoxy intermediates that are further converted to epoxide and dihydroxy products, with cyclooxygenase-2 in its aspirin-acetylated form providing an alternative entry. Failure of this resolution arm is associated with persistent, non-resolving inflammation in chronic disease.

Meiotic recombination is how homologous chromosomes exchange DNA during gamete formation, shuffling alleles between parental chromosomes and, just as importantly, physically tethering each homolog pair so that the first meiotic division segregates them correctly. Without at least one crossover per bivalent, chromosomes missegregate, producing aneuploid eggs and sperm, infertility and pregnancy loss. The process begins with programmed double-strand breaks made by SPO11, whose covalent attachment to the DNA is removed nucleolytically before the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and its partner RBBP8 resect the ends. RPA-coated 3' overhangs are handed to the RecA-like strand exchange proteins RAD51 and DMC1, aided by MND1 and PSMC3IP, which invade the homolog. Most intermediates resolve without crossover; a minority mature through MSH4-MSH5 and MLH1-MLH3 into chiasmata. PRDM9 marks hotspots by methylating histones, targeting breaks to defined genomic positions.

Oxidative attack on DNA leaves lesions that must be excised before they block replication or cause mutation, and the glycosylase NEIL3 is the enzyme that initiates that removal in a particular niche: single-stranded DNA, telomeric repeats, and replication forks. It cleaves hydantoin products of guanine oxidation and thymine glycol, and also unhooks certain interstrand crosslinks independently of the Fanconi anaemia route, so loss of activity leaves both oxidative base damage and crosslinks unresolved. Failure of this arm of base excision repair has consequences beyond mutagenesis: an inactivating variant predisposes to autoimmune disease, depletion accelerates telomere loss, and deficiency limits proliferation of neural stem cells and adult hippocampal neurogenesis, with learning and memory deficits. Expression rises in failing heart and atherosclerotic plaque, where its protective role appears only partly explained by DNA repair.

Maturation of the SARS-CoV-2 envelope (E) protein covers the post-translational modifications that convert the newly translated viral protein into its functional, membrane-associated form. E is a small hydrophobic protein that accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and ERGIC membranes, where it contributes to virion assembly, budding and the ion-channel (porin-like) activity attributed to E trimers rather than trafficking to the plasma membrane. After synthesis the protein is palmitoylated on cysteines, which stabilises its membrane interaction, and is ubiquitinated using the host ubiquitin pool supplied by the ribosomal fusion precursors and polyubiquitin genes represented here. Because correctly matured E is required for efficient production of infectious particles and for the membrane remodelling that accompanies coronaviral egress, this step links host protein-modification machinery to the late stages of the viral replication cycle and to candidate antiviral targets.

Internal tandem duplications in the FLT3 receptor tyrosine kinase are among the most common lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia, and one reason they transform cells is that the mutant kinase, unlike the wild-type receptor, drives strong constitutive STAT5 activation. This gives leukaemic blasts a growth and survival signal that no longer requires ligand, and it is the arm of FLT3 signalling most closely tied to disease aggressiveness and to response or resistance to kinase inhibitors. The mislocalised, autophosphorylated receptor recruits GRB2 and the scaffold GAB2 together with the phosphatase PTPN11, phosphorylating STAT5A and STAT5B so they dimerise and enter the nucleus. There they induce targets that push proliferation and block death, including the anti-apoptotic BCL2L1 and the kinase PIM1, alongside altered CDKN1A control of the cell cycle and NOX4-derived reactive oxygen species that sustain the signal.

RHOBTB3 looks like a small GTPase but behaves differently: its nucleotide-binding domain hydrolyses ATP rather than GTP, and the cycling of this atypical Rho-family protein drives membrane traffic and targeted protein degradation. It works on Golgi membranes and endosomes, where it cooperates with RAB9 to return cargo from late endosomes to the trans-Golgi network, and it is anchored by a C-terminal prenylation motif not found in its RHOBTB1 and RHOBTB2 relatives. Through its tandem BTB domains it serves as a substrate adaptor for CUL3-based ubiquitin ligases, delivering targets such as cyclin E for degradation and thereby restraining cell cycle progression; it also feeds into the hypoxic response alongside VHL. Loss of RHOBTB3 expression is common in tumours, consistent with a tumour-suppressive role linking vesicular transport, ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis and proliferative control.

Late in infection by enveloped viruses, the same fusion machinery that mediates entry can merge neighbouring cells into multinucleated syncytia, and this describes that induction of cell-cell fusion. In SARS-CoV-2 infection, spike displayed on the surface of an infected cell engages ACE2 on a neighbour, generating synapse-like contacts that progress to a fusion pore and cytoplasmic continuity; infected syncytial pneumocytes are a hallmark of severe COVID-19 lung pathology. Proteolytic priming of spike by the cell-surface protease TMPRSS2 and by furin at the S1/S2 boundary raises fusion efficiency, and several variants fuse more readily. Anoctamin family members contribute as calcium-activated chloride channels and phospholipid scramblases, with ANO6-type scrambling exposing phosphatidylserine to destabilise the bilayer and permit lipid mixing. Syncytia are thought to aid replication, immune evasion, and internalisation of lymphocytes.

Adipogenesis is the differentiation of precursor cells into fat cells, the storage depot and endocrine organ that buffers systemic energy supply; when it fails or is overwhelmed, lipid spills into liver and muscle and insulin resistance follows, while its extremes produce lipodystrophy or obesity. The programme is transcriptional at heart: CEBPB and CEBPD initiate, then PPARG with its RXRA partner and CEBPA lock in the mature state, driving the lipid-handling machinery of white adipocytes such as FABP4, CD36, LPL, PLIN1, GLUT4 and the hormones leptin and adiponectin. Coactivators and Mediator subunits, acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300, and repressive NCOR/HDAC and NuRD complexes tune this output; WNT and TGF-beta signals restrain it. A parallel branch specified by PRDM16, EBF2 and PPARGC1A yields thermogenic brown and beige cells expressing UCP1, CIDEA and DIO2 for heat production.

Cells continuously read the physical forces around them — blood flow shear, tissue stretch, matrix stiffness, touch — and convert them into chemical signals, and this conversion is what allows endothelium to align with laminar flow, osteocytes to remodel bone under load, and sensory structures to register mechanical contact. Force-gated channels such as PIEZO1 and TRPV4 admit calcium, while integrins (ITGA5, ITGAV, ITGB1) coupled through talin, vinculin and focal adhesion kinase transmit tension from fibronectin and the matrix into the cytoskeleton. Downstream, PI3K–AKT–mTOR complexes, adenylyl cyclase and PKA, NF-κB subunits, and the transcriptional coactivator YAP1 translate the stimulus into changes in gene expression, growth and survival; PECAM1, CDH5 and eNOS carry the endothelial arm toward vasodilation. Purinergic release through pannexin and P2 receptors amplifies the response, and NLRP3 links excessive force to inflammation. Disturbed mechanotransduction contributes to atherosclerosis at flow-disturbed sites, fibrosis and disuse bone loss.

Dengue virus carries a tiny genome and must borrow host machinery to replicate and to blunt the immune response, and these virus-host interactions describe where its proteins go and what they grab. Viral products made in the cytosol, ER and ER-Golgi intermediate compartment then reach the nucleus, mitochondria and, in the case of secreted NS1, the bloodstream, where NS1 enters uninfected cells and reprograms innate and adaptive immunity. The host partners here fall into recognisable blocks: spliceosome, RNA polymerase II, cleavage and polyadenylation and hnRNP/SR proteins, suggesting extensive hijacking of nuclear mRNA processing; RIG-I-like and STING-dependent sensing, complement components and TLR4/MD-2 signalling, which the virus suppresses; mTOR complexes and autophagy initiators that support replication; and junctional and glycocalyx proteins including ZO-1, syndecans and glypicans, whose disruption contributes to the vascular leak of dengue hemorrhagic fever.

Antibody responses improve over days to weeks because germinal center B cells are repeatedly tested for how tightly their receptors bind antigen, and only the best binders survive. This affinity selection of immunoglobulins is what converts a low-affinity naive repertoire into high-affinity, class-switched antibody, and its failure underlies poor vaccine responses, immunodeficiency, and, when selection is subverted, autoantibodies and B cell lymphoma. Antigen held as immune complexes on follicular dendritic cells via complement receptors CR1/CR2 and FCGR2B is extracted by high-affinity receptors using non-muscle myosin IIa, then processed by cathepsins and presented on MHC class II to follicular helper T cells, whose CD40L, IL4 and IL21 grant survival. Selected cells cycle back for AICDA-driven hypermutation, requiring mismatch repair, translesion polymerases and BCL6-centred transcriptional control.
